claim: Cortical lesions represent a hallmark of multiple sclerosis.
source: Cortical lesions represent a hallmark of multiple sclerosis and are proposed as a predictor of disease severity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Cortical lesions are proposed as a predictor of disease severity in multiple sclerosis.
source: Cortical lesions represent a hallmark of multiple sclerosis and are proposed as a predictor of disease severity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Filippi and Rocca, 2019; Filippi et al., 2010; Treaba et al., 2019).

claim: microRNAs are suggested to be important players in multiple sclerosis disease pathogenesis.
source: microRNAs are suggested to be important players in the disease pathogenesis and the experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis animal model.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Junker et al., 2011; Thamilarasan et al., 2012).

claim: The implemented mouse model is characterized by both an autoimmune heterogeneity and the presence of cortical lesions.
source: We implemented a mouse model recapitulating more closely the human pathology as it is characterized by both an autoimmune heterogeneity and the presence of cortical lesions, two parameters missing in experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through experimental data presented in the results section.

claim: Mice clustered in two groups displaying high or low clinical scores in the model.
source: In our model, mice clustered in two groups displaying high or low clinical scores.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by data in Figure 1A showing HIS and LIS groups.

claim: Upon cortical cytokine injection, lesions appeared with a specific topography.
source: Upon cortical cytokine injection, lesions appeared with a specific topography while cortical miRNA profiles were altered.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by data in Figures 3 and 4 showing lesion distribution.

claim: Cortical miRNA profiles were altered upon cortical cytokine injection.
source: Upon cortical cytokine injection, lesions appeared with a specific topography while cortical miRNA profiles were altered.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by miRNA profiling data in Figure 6 and Supplementary files.

claim: Lesion topography and miRNA profiles differed according to disease severity.
source: These two features differed according to disease severity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by comparing HIS-C and LIS-C groups in Figures 3, 4, and 6.

claim: Changes in miRNA regulators and targets suggest that miRNA alteration had functional repercussions.
source: We evidenced changes in miRNA regulators and targets suggesting that miRNA alteration had functional repercussions that could explain the differences in cortical lesions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 7 showing FOXO3, C1q, and target gene expression.

claim: Multiple sclerosis pathogenesis is proposed to be the consequence of an interplay between genetic susceptibility and environmental factors.
source: It is proposed to be the consequence of an interplay between genetic susceptibility and environmental factors (e.g. low vitamin D levels, smoking, Epstein-Barr virus infection).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: MS is a complex and heterogeneous disease presenting various degrees of inflammation, gliosis, and neurodegeneration.
source: MS is a complex and heterogeneous disease presenting various degrees of inflammation, gliosis, and neurodegeneration leading to differences in clinical manifestations and severity between patients (Paz Soldan and Rodriguez, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Progress in imaging put forth the relevance of lesions in the gray matter, particularly in the cerebral cortex.
source: For decades, the focus in MS was on white matter lesions, however, progress in imaging put forth the relevance of lesions in the gray matter, particularly in the cerebral cortex (Filippi and Rocca, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Cortical lesions are now established as a hallmark of MS.
source: It is now established that these cortical lesions (CLs) represent a hallmark of MS (Lucchinetti et al., 2011; Filippi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The presence of cortical lesions in patients with a clinically isolated syndrome is suggested as a confirmation for MS diagnosis.
source: Actually, the presence of CLs in patients with a clinically isolated syndrome is suggested as a confirmation for MS diagnosis (Filippi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: The assessment of cortical lesions has been added to the diagnostic criteria of MS.
source: Accordingly, the assessment of CLs has been added to the diagnostic criteria of MS (Thompson et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Meningeal inflammation and immune cell infiltration play a role in the development of cortical lesions.
source: However, it has been suggested that meningeal inflammation and immune cell infiltration, characterized by the presence of T-cell infiltrates, B-cells, and macrophages play a role in the development of CLs (Treaba et al., 2019; Howell et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Oxidative stress leading to DNA damage and degeneration of oligodendrocytes and neurons could be implicated in cortical lesion formation.
source: Besides inflammation, oxidative stress leading to DNA damage, and degeneration of oligodendrocytes and neurons, could also be implicated in CL formation (Fischer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: The direct involvement of microRNAs in MS pathogenesis has been put forth.
source: Recently, the direct involvement of microRNAs (miRNAs) in MS pathogenesis (Junker et al., 2011), as well as in the pathogenesis of the experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) animal model has been put forth (Thamilarasan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: miRNAs are small non-coding RNA that mediate the repression of messenger RNA translation.
source: miRNAs are small non-coding RNA that mediate the repression of messenger RNA translation and thereby refine protein expression levels.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents established knowledge.

claim: Up to 60% of protein-coding genes are regulated by miRNAs.
source: It is estimated that up to 60% of protein-coding genes are regulated by miRNAs (Friedman et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Dysregulation of the miRNA profile was reported in the peripheral blood of MS patients.
source: Dysregulation of the miRNA profile was reported in the peripheral blood (Keller et al., 2014), in active and inactive lesions, and in normal-appearing white matter in MS patients (Junker et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Dysregulation of the miRNA profile was reported in active and inactive lesions in MS patients.
source: Dysregulation of the miRNA profile was reported in the peripheral blood (Keller et al., 2014), in active and inactive lesions, and in normal-appearing white matter in MS patients (Junker et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Mice that received PTX declared the disease earlier than mice that did not.
source: As might be expected, mice that received the PTX declared the disease earlier than mice that did not (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 1A.

claim: EAE mice that did not receive PTX could be separated into two distinct cohorts: mice with a high clinical score (HIS; 53% of the immunized mice) and mice with a low clinical score (LIS; 47%).
source: Using a standard five-point EAE grading scale, we could separate the EAE mice that did not receive PTX into two distinct cohorts (Figure 1A): mice with a high clinical score (HIS; 53% of the immunized mice) and mice with a low clinical score (LIS; 47%).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 1A.

claim: There was no difference in disease onset between the HIS and LIS groups.
source: Importantly, there was no difference in disease onset between the HIS and LIS groups.
evidence: This is stated in the results and can be inferred from Figure 1A.

claim: Decreased fluoromyelin staining was observed in the spinal cord of EAE mice.
source: Accordingly, we could observe decreased fluoromyelin staining in the spinal cord of EAE mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 1B.

claim: There were less lesions in the LIS group compared to the HIS group in the spinal cord.
source: We also found less lesions in the LIS group compared to the HIS group, and that the latter could not be distinguished from the PTX group.
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 1B.

claim: The decrease in fluoromyelin staining was more marked in the HIS group compared to the LIS group.
source: Indeed, the decrease in fluoromyelin staining was more marked in the HIS group compared to the LIS group, consistent with the higher clinical score (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 1B.

claim: The same immunization protocol without PTX conducted on a second independent set of mice showed two distinct phenotypes (HIS and LIS) with a similar distribution.
source: To assess reproducibility and strengthen our findings, the same immunization protocol without PTX was conducted on a second independent set of mice (different suppliers and laboratories). Here again, we observed two distinct phenotypes, that is HIS and LIS, with a similar distribution (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Decreased Luxol Fast Blue-Cresyl Violet staining was observed in the spinal cord of both HIS and LIS mice of the second cohort.
source: This was accompanied by decreased Luxol Fast Blue-Cresyl Violet (LFB-CV) staining in the spinal cord of both HIS and LIS mice of this second cohort.
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CD3 immunostaining in all the mice that received the immunizing peptide was similar.
source: CD3 immunostaining in all the mice that received the immunizing peptide was similar (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Larger Iba-1-occupied areas were found in the HIS group compared to the LIS group in both white and grey matters of the spinal cord.
source: We found, both in the white and grey matters, larger Iba-1-occupied and GFAP-positive areas in the HIS group compared to the LIS group (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 1E-G.

claim: Larger GFAP-positive areas were found in the HIS group compared to the LIS group in both white and grey matters of the spinal cord.
source: We found, both in the white and grey matters, larger Iba-1-occupied and GFAP-positive areas in the HIS group compared to the LIS group (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 1E-G.

claim: Immunization resulted in an increased mRNA expression of cytokines, chemokines, and Foxp3 in the spinal cord.
source: Immunization resulted in an increased mRNA expression of cytokines, chemokines, and Foxp3 and a decreased expression of Rorc (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 2A.

claim: Immunization resulted in a decreased expression of Rorc in the spinal cord.
source: Immunization resulted in an increased mRNA expression of cytokines, chemokines, and Foxp3 and a decreased expression of Rorc (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 2A.

claim: Foxp3 was more expressed in the LIS group compared to the HIS group in the spinal cord.
source: There were no differences between the HIS and LIS groups, except for Foxp3 which was more expressed in the LIS group compared to the HIS group (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 2A.

claim: Circulating cytokine levels were similar in the HIS and LIS groups, except for IL-12p40 at day 14 and MIP-1α at day 21.
source: Circulating cytokine levels were similar in the HIS and LIS groups, except for IL-12p40 at day 14 and MIP-1α at day 21.
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Increased mRNA expression of Il1b, Tnf, and Cxcl10 was found in the immunized groups compared to the control group in the cortex.
source: Therefore, we measured the mRNA expression of cytokines and chemokines and found increased mRNA expression of Il1b, Tnf, and Cxcl10 in the immunized groups compared to the control group (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 2B.

claim: Tnf was more expressed in the HIS group compared to the LIS group in the cortex.
source: Interestingly, the cytokine Tnf and the chemokine Cxcl10 were more expressed in the HIS group compared to the LIS group (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 2B.

claim: Cxcl10 was more expressed in the HIS group compared to the LIS group in the cortex.
source: Interestingly, the cytokine Tnf and the chemokine Cxcl10 were more expressed in the HIS group compared to the LIS group (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 2B.

claim: Cd3g mRNA was more expressed in the HIS group compared to the LIS group in the cortex.
source: This was also the case for mRNA of the lymphocyte marker Cd3g (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 2B.

claim: Decreased expression of Bdnf was found in the immunized groups compared to the control group in the cortex.
source: When looking at the expression of neurotrophic factors, we found decreased expression of Bdnf in the immunized groups compared to the control group with no difference between HIS and LIS (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 2C.

claim: Gdnf expression was increased only in the groups that did not receive PTX in the cortex.
source: Gdnf expression on the other hand was increased only in the groups that did not receive PTX with higher expression in the HIS group compared to the LIS group (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 2C.

claim: Gdnf expression was higher in the HIS group compared to the LIS group in the cortex.
source: Gdnf expression on the other hand was increased only in the groups that did not receive PTX with higher expression in the HIS group compared to the LIS group (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 2C.

claim: Stereotactic injection of TNFα and IFNγ into the primary somatosensory cortex of EAE mice on day 21 post-immunization was performed to induce cortical lesions.
source: To induce these CLs in mice, we stereotactically injected TNFα and IFNγ into the primary somatosensory cortex of EAE mice (both HIS and LIS groups) on day 21 post-immunization and sacrificed them 3 days after (time needed for the potential CLs to form Gardner et al., 2013; Merkler et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations.

claim: Decreased LFB-CV staining was found in the ipsilateral cortices of both HIS-Cytokine and LIS-Cytokine mice but not in the EAE mice injected with PBS.
source: When analyzing the cortex of these mice, we found decreased LFB-CV staining in the ipsilateral cortices of both HIS-Cytokine (HIS-C) and LIS-Cytokine (LIS-C) mice but not in the EAE mice injected with PBS (HIS-PBS and LIS-PBS) (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 3A-C.

claim: The decreased LFB-CV staining was more marked in the HIS-C group compared to the LIS-C group.
source: The decreased LFB-CV staining was more marked in the HIS-C group compared to the LIS-C group (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 3B.

claim: Fluoromyelin signal intensity was lower in the HIS-C group compared to the LIS-C group in the ipsilateral cortex.
source: Indeed, fluoromyelin signal intensity was lower in the HIS-C group compared to the LIS-C group in the ipsilateral cortex (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 3D-E.

claim: Lower cortical myelin basic protein signal was found in the HIS-C group compared to the LIS-C.
source: This was further confirmed by lower cortical myelin basic protein (MBP) signal in the HIS-C group compared to the LIS-C (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 3F.

claim: Fluoromyelin signal intensity was not changed in the ipsilateral cortices of PBS injected groups compared to the control mice.
source: Moreover, fluoromyelin signal intensity was not changed in the ipsilateral cortices of PBS injected groups compared to the control mice (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 3B.

claim: A large number of cortical lesions were evidenced in the somatosensory cortex in both HIS-C and LIS-C groups.
source: In both groups, we evidenced a large number of CLs in the somatosensory cortex and in the motor and visual cortices albeit with a lower frequency than in the somatosensory cortex (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Cortical lesions were found in the motor and visual cortices with a lower frequency than in the somatosensory cortex.
source: In both groups, we evidenced a large number of CLs in the somatosensory cortex and in the motor and visual cortices albeit with a lower frequency than in the somatosensory cortex (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 4A-C.

claim: No difference in cortical lesion distribution was found between the HIS-C and LIS-C groups.
source: However, we found no difference in CL distribution between the HIS-C and LIS-C groups (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 4A-C.

claim: MBP-negative area in intracortical and subpial cortical lesions was higher in the HIS-C group compared to the LIS-C group.
source: MBP-negative area in intracortical and subpial CLs was higher in the HIS-C group compared to the LIS-C group (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 4D-F.

claim: GFAP staining in both HIS-C and LIS-C mice was increased around the lesion site, showing prominent astrogliosis.
source: GFAP staining in both HIS-C and LIS-C mice was increased around the lesion site, showing prominent astrogliosis (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 3G.

claim: Iba-1 staining showed no difference between HIS-C and LIS-C mice.
source: Conversely, Iba-1 staining showed no difference between HIS-C and LIS-C mice (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 4G.

claim: No difference in CD3 positive cells was found between the HIS-C and LIS-C mice in the cortex.
source: We found no difference between the HIS-C and LIS-C mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cortical areas with a decrease in toluidine blue staining were found, but no difference between the HIS and LIS groups.
source: We found cortical areas with a decrease in toluidine blue staining, but no difference between the HIS and LIS groups (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The extent of LFB staining loss was not affected by the timing of cytokine injection.
source: Interestingly, the extent of LFB staining loss was not affected by the timing of cytokine injection (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 4J.

claim: mRNA expression of Il1b, Tnf, Ifng, and Cd3g were not different between the three groups (LIS-C, HIS-C, HIS-C-35).
source: Furthermore, mRNA expression of the cytokines Il1b, Tnf, and Ifng and expression of the lymphocyte marker Cd3g were not different between the three groups (LIS-C, HIS-C, HIS-C-35) (Figure 4K).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 4K.

claim: The expression of Atf3 was lower in the HIS-C group compared to the LIS-C group.
source: However, the expression of Atf3 (activating transcription factor 3), a marker of cellular stress, was lower while the expression of the neurotrophin Ntf3 was higher in the HIS-C group compared to the LIS-C group (Figure 4K).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 4K.

claim: The expression of the neurotrophin Ntf3 was higher in the HIS-C group compared to the LIS-C group.
source: However, the expression of Atf3 (activating transcription factor 3), a marker of cellular stress, was lower while the expression of the neurotrophin Ntf3 was higher in the HIS-C group compared to the LIS-C group (Figure 4K).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 4K.

claim: A decrease in Ifnb mRNA expression was found in the HIS-C-35 group compared to the other two groups.
source: Concerning the HIS-C-35 group, we only found a decrease in Ifnb mRNA expression compared to the other two groups (Figure 4K).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 4K.

claim: Cytokine injection increased the mRNA expression of Il1b, Tnf, Cxcl10, Atf3, Ngf, and Ntf3 in both LIS and HIS groups.
source: Our data show that cytokine injection increased the mRNA expression of Il1b, Tnf, Cxcl10, Atf3, Ngf, and Ntf3 in both LIS and HIS groups (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 5.

claim: Bdnf was decreased in LIS-C compared to LIS mice.
source: Conversely, Bdnf was decreased in LIS-C compared to LIS mice while Gdnf was decreased in HIS-C compared to HIS mice (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 5.

claim: Gdnf was decreased in HIS-C compared to HIS mice.
source: Conversely, Bdnf was decreased in LIS-C compared to LIS mice while Gdnf was decreased in HIS-C compared to HIS mice (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 5.

claim: Cd3g mRNA expression was increased in the LIS-C group compared to the LIS group but not in the HIS-C group.
source: Finally, Cd3g mRNA expression was increased in the LIS-C group compared to the LIS group but not in the HIS-C group (Figure 5), suggesting that cytokine injection increased lymphocyte infiltration in the LIS group.
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 5.

claim: 202 miRNAs were expressed in the ipsilateral cortex of HIS-C mice.
source: We found 202 miRNAs expressed in the ipsilateral and 197 miRNAs in the contralateral side of HIS-C mice, 197 miRNAs in the ipsilateral, and 179 miRNAs in the contralateral of LIS-C mice, and 167 miRNAs expressed in control mice (i.e. PBS-injected non EAE mice, CTL).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: 197 miRNAs were expressed in the contralateral cortex of HIS-C mice.
source: We found 202 miRNAs expressed in the ipsilateral and 197 miRNAs in the contralateral side of HIS-C mice, 197 miRNAs in the ipsilateral, and 179 miRNAs in the contralateral of LIS-C mice, and 167 miRNAs expressed in control mice (i.e. PBS-injected non EAE mice, CTL).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: 197 miRNAs were expressed in the ipsilateral cortex of LIS-C mice.
source: We found 202 miRNAs expressed in the ipsilateral and 197 miRNAs in the contralateral side of HIS-C mice, 197 miRNAs in the ipsilateral, and 179 miRNAs in the contralateral of LIS-C mice, and 167 miRNAs expressed in control mice (i.e. PBS-injected non EAE mice, CTL).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: 179 miRNAs were expressed in the contralateral cortex of LIS-C mice.
source: We found 202 miRNAs expressed in the ipsilateral and 197 miRNAs in the contralateral side of HIS-C mice, 197 miRNAs in the ipsilateral, and 179 miRNAs in the contralateral of LIS-C mice, and 167 miRNAs expressed in control mice (i.e. PBS-injected non EAE mice, CTL).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: 167 miRNAs were expressed in control mice.
source: We found 202 miRNAs expressed in the ipsilateral and 197 miRNAs in the contralateral side of HIS-C mice, 197 miRNAs in the ipsilateral, and 179 miRNAs in the contralateral of LIS-C mice, and 167 miRNAs expressed in control mice (i.e. PBS-injected non EAE mice, CTL).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: A subset of 155 miRNAs was expressed in all samples.
source: A subset of 155 miRNAs was expressed in all samples (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: For the ipsilateral injected structure of HIS-C versus CTL, 161 miRNAs were expressed in both groups and among them, 139 were upregulated, and none were downregulated.
source: Analysis of the ipsilateral injected structure of HIS-C versus CTL showed 161 miRNAs were expressed in both groups and among them, 139 were upregulated, and none were downregulated.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: For the contralateral cortical structure of HIS-C, 161 miRNAs were expressed in both HIS-C and CTL of which 138 were upregulated and two were downregulated.
source: For the corresponding contralateral cortical structure of HIS-C, 161 miRNAs were expressed in both HIS-C and CTL of which 138 were upregulated and two were downregulated.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: For the ipsilateral injected structure of LIS-C versus CTL, 160 miRNAs were expressed in both groups and among them, 127 were upregulated, and four were downregulated.
source: Analysis of the ipsilateral injected structure of LIS-C versus CTL showed 160 miRNAs expressed in both groups and among them, 127 were upregulated, and four were downregulated.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: For the contralateral cortical structure of LIS-C, 157 miRNAs were expressed in both LIS-C and CTL of which 115 were upregulated and two were downregulated.
source: For the corresponding contralateral cortical structure of LIS-C, 157 miRNAs were expressed in both LIS-C and CTL of which 115 were upregulated and two were downregulated.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: EAE induces miRNA expression compared to the control group in the cortical region surrounding the injection site.
source: These data suggest that, in the cortical region surrounding the injection site, EAE induces miRNA expression compared to the control group as more miRNAs were expressed in the HIS-C and LIS-C groups compared to CTL, and many of the miRNAs expressed in all groups were up-regulated compared to the control group (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: 192 miRNAs were expressed when comparing the ipsilateral cortical region surrounding the injection site of HIS-C and LIS-C mice, 20 of which were more expressed in HIS-C, and eight were less expressed.
source: We found 192 miRNAs expressed, 20 of which were more expressed in HIS-C, and eight were less expressed.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Supplementary file 3.

claim: When comparing the contralateral corresponding cortical structure of HIS-C and LIS-C mice, 177 miRNAs were expressed, 59 of them were more expressed in HIS-C compared to LIS-C while only one miRNA was less expressed.
source: We also compared the miRNA profiles between the contralateral corresponding cortical structure of HIS-C and LIS-C mice (Supplementary file 3). In this case, we found 177 miRNAs expressed, 59 of them were more expressed in HIS-C compared to LIS-C while only one miRNA was less expressed.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Supplementary file 3.

claim: In silico analysis predicted the involvement of altered miRNAs in several pathways known to be involved in MS including neurotrophin signaling, FoxO signaling and T cell signaling.
source: In silico analysis on the miRNAs that were altered in HIS-C-ipsi vs LIS-C-ipsi or were found only in either HIS-C-ipsi or LIS-C-ipsi predicted the involvement of these microRNAs in several pathways known to be involved in MS (Figure 6C) including neurotrophin signaling, FoxO signaling and T cell signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 6C.

claim: Four of the altered miRNAs (Mir152-3p, Mir7b-5p, Mir148a-3p, and Mir7a-5p) had Mbp as target gene.
source: Indeed, four of the altered miRNAs (Mir152-3p, Mir7b-5p, Mir148a-3p, and Mir7a-5p) had Mbp as target gene (Figure 6D) and could, therefore, play a role in myelination.
evidence: This is stated in the results and demonstrated by data in Figure 6D.

claim: FOXO3 could be targeted by three of the differentially altered miRNAs: Mir155-5p, Mir223-3p, and Mir29b-3p.
source: Another interesting gene in these pathways is the gene for the transcription factor FOXO3, which could be targeted by three of the differentially altered miRNAs: Mir155-5p, Mir223-3p, and Mir29b-3p.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by in silico analysis.

claim: FOXO3 controls Th1 cell differentiation.
source: Indeed, while this transcription factor is not yet extensively studied in the context of MS, FOXO3 controls Th1 cell differentiation, inhibits oligodendrocyte progenitor cell differentiation, and was shown to exert an important role in neuroinflammation (Stienne et al., 2016; Srivastava et al., 2018; Stefanetti et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations.

claim: FOXO3 inhibits oligodendrocyte progenitor cell differentiation.
source: Indeed, while this transcription factor is not yet extensively studied in the context of MS, FOXO3 controls Th1 cell differentiation, inhibits oligodendrocyte progenitor cell differentiation, and was shown to exert an important role in neuroinflammation (Stienne et al., 2016; Srivastava et al., 2018; Stefanetti et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations.

claim: FOXO3 exerts an important role in neuroinflammation.
source: Indeed, while this transcription factor is not yet extensively studied in the context of MS, FOXO3 controls Th1 cell differentiation, inhibits oligodendrocyte progenitor cell differentiation, and was shown to exert an important role in neuroinflammation (Stienne et al., 2016; Srivastava et al., 2018; Stefanetti et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations.

claim: Foxo3-deficient mice exhibit reduced susceptibility to EAE.
source: Moreover, Foxo3-deficient mice exhibit reduced susceptibility to EAE (Stienne et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citation.

claim: Mir29b-3p was expressed in the ipsilateral cortical structure surrounding the injection site of LIS-C-ipsi but not in HIS-C-ipsi.
source: Here, we observed that Mir29b-3p was expressed in the ipsilateral cortical structure surrounding the injection site of LIS-C-ipsi but not in HIS-C-ipsi.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Mir155-5p and Mir223-3p were upregulated in the injection site of HIS-C and LIS-C groups compared to CTL.
source: Mir155-5p and Mir223-3p were upregulated in the injection site of HIS-C and LIS-C groups compared to CTL.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The upregulation of Mir155-5p was stronger in LIS-C than in HIS-C.
source: The upregulation was stronger in LIS-C than in HIS-C for Mir155-5p but the opposite was true for Mir223-3p (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The upregulation of Mir223-3p was stronger in HIS-C than in LIS-C.
source: The upregulation was stronger in LIS-C than in HIS-C for Mir155-5p but the opposite was true for Mir223-3p (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: When comparing HIS-C-ipsi versus LIS-C-ipsi, Mir155-5p was less expressed in HIS-C, while Mir223-3p was more expressed.
